questions.text: What is the number of states in the minimal DFA over {0, 1} accepting all strings in which the number of 0s is divisible by 2 and the number of 1s is divisible by 3?
questions.explain: The product construction tracks (count of 0s mod 2, count of 1s mod 3), giving 2 x 3 = 6 states. All six are reachable and pairwise distinguishable, so the minimal DFA has 6 states.

questions.text: What is the number of states in the minimal DFA over {0, 1} that accepts binary strings, read most significant bit first, whose value is divisible by 5? The empty string is not accepted.
questions.explain: Track the remainder modulo 5 as each bit is consumed: state r moves to (2r + b) mod 5. Five residue classes, all reachable and distinguishable, so 5 states.

questions.text: Which of the following languages over {a, b} are regular? Select all that apply.
options: Strings where the number of a's equals the number of b's
Strings of length divisible by 7
Strings where the number of a's minus the number of b's is at most 3 in absolute value
Strings containing aba as a substring
questions.explain: Equal counts needs unbounded counting and fails the pumping lemma. Length mod 7 needs 7 states. A bounded difference needs only finitely many counter values, so it is regular. Substring search is regular.

questions.text: Context-free languages are closed under which of the following operations? Select all that apply.
options: Union
Intersection
Concatenation
Intersection with a regular language
questions.explain: CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, Kleene star and intersection with a regular language. They are not closed under intersection with another CFL, nor under complement.

questions.text: Which language is context-free but not regular?
options: Strings of a's and b's of even length
a^n b^n for n >= 0
a^n b^n c^n for n >= 0
Strings over {a, b} ending in ab
questions.explain: a^n b^n needs a stack but no more, so it is context-free and not regular. a^n b^n c^n requires two independent counters and is not context-free. The other two are regular.

questions.text: Which statement about deterministic pushdown automata (DPDA) is true?
options: Every CFL is accepted by some DPDA
DPDAs accept exactly the deterministic CFLs, a strict subset of the CFLs
DPDAs and NPDAs accept exactly the same class of languages
DPDAs accept exactly the regular languages
questions.explain: Unlike finite automata, determinism restricts pushdown automata strictly. The language of even-length palindromes is context-free but not accepted by any DPDA.

questions.text: Which of the following problems are decidable? Select all that apply.
options: Given a DFA, is the language it accepts empty?
Given two DFAs, do they accept the same language?
Given a CFG, is the language it generates empty?
Given two CFGs, do they generate the same language?
questions.explain: DFA emptiness and equivalence are decidable, as is CFG emptiness (test whether the start symbol is generating). CFG equivalence is undecidable, as is CFL intersection emptiness.

questions.text: A language L and its complement are both Turing-recognisable (recursively enumerable). What follows?
options: L is decidable
L is regular
L is context-free
Nothing further can be concluded
questions.explain: Run both recognisers in parallel. One of them must halt and accept, so the answer is always reached in finite time. Hence L is recursive, i.e. decidable.

questions.text: By the Myhill-Nerode theorem, a language L is regular if and only if:
options: L is generated by some context-free grammar
The number of equivalence classes of the relation induced by L on strings is finite
L is accepted by some nondeterministic pushdown automaton
L is closed under concatenation
questions.explain: Two strings are equivalent when no suffix distinguishes them. L is regular exactly when this relation has finitely many classes, and that count equals the number of states in the minimal DFA.
